results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 34 aligned units summarise to the controlling idea of their spec paragraph, including the revised p08 (two alternatives plus a division that combines with either) and p19 (decision list as the author's extension); the three callouts match no spec paragraph by design.

Two units were marked two_ideas (hardest-join pattern para 3 = p15, AI para 2 = p29). In both the spec's controlling idea deliberately joins the two things (each change exposing the next plus the one late change; a new role plus a changed configuration, both under 'open'), so neither is a failure.
Every unit serves the supporting claim its section declares (S1 scene and definitions, S2 configurations, S3 choice, S4 first team, S5 the three reporting lines, S6 AI); no unit stands outside S1-S6.

Each table has a lead-in or a following paragraph saying what it shows (six roles in one line each; the mapping as the author's position; each change answering one join and exposing the next; the page replacing the drawings), the figure's three diagrams are each read in a paragraph, and the Lencioni quotation and Larson's observations are tied to Corvane's three teams with two plans.

Sourced concepts name book and concept (Larson's Primer for the engineering executive and structured escalation, credited on to LinkedIn; An Elegant Puzzle and Five Dysfunctions for first team; Build What Matters for the Throne Room); the product-executive rule is presented as that book's rule of thumb; the author's extensions and judgments are marked (the first-team reading, the decision list, the configuration mapping, the three reporting sections). The Larson zero-sum remark and the Lencioni quote in the second first-team paragraph rely on the book named one paragraph earlier, which is adequate.

Every declared transition_in is expressed at its boundary, mostly in the opening sentence (e.g. 'What the drawings left unstated can be stated', 'The second diagram is the opposite', 'Peers need the principle because of what happens without it', 'Data is placed by the same rule'). The AI section opens with the label note and gives the transition in its second sentence, which still reads as declared.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Make the Executive Team the First Team ¶2
results.quote: At Corvane, one undefined word between two executives became three teams with two plans each.
results.finding: Both readers could not tell which word was meant and went back to the scene section to find 'leading a team'. Naming the word here would remove the trip back.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Choose the Configuration from the Hardest Join ¶1
results.quote: Choose the configuration that puts a person, or a written agreement between two people, on that join.
results.finding: Both readers found that the procedure identifies only the hardest join: when it is product with engineering, peers and one combined executive both satisfy step 4 and nothing sends the reader to balance versus speed. The spec's own steps for p13 stop at the same point while the section transition promises 'how to find which condition a company is in'; a clause in step 4 pointing to the mapping table would close it without reordering.

results.quote: Priya Nambiar, the new chief product officer (CPO)
results.finding: Both readers took 'new' to mean an outside hire and were surprised when the history table called her the first product manager from 2020; reader A went back to check, reader B resolved it in place, so it is minor. A word saying she was promoted would fix it.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Choose the Configuration from the Hardest Join ¶4
results.quote: After 2023 Tomas Rell's role was partly this: a founder who kept his title while Dario Vance ran engineering, with nothing written about the split.
results.finding: Both readers read 'this' as the Throne Room (not letting go of product decisions) when it means a role made to keep a person; both resolved it by re-reading, so it is minor.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Make the Executive Team the First Team ¶1
results.quote: in the *Primer* he calls the weekly leadership meeting the forum for forging an executive's direct reports into one
results.finding: Both readers needed a second read: 'one' has a distant antecedent, and the example points at the executive's own reports one sentence after the definition pointed the other way. Rated (b) by both, so minor.

results.quote: By this chapter's rule, a head of AI is warranted only where there is a join that no existing role can make
results.finding: Both readers noted that no rule was stated in this form: 'the rule' in the three preceding sections was the reporting rule, and this one has to be assembled from 'read a role by the decisions it makes'. Rated (b) by both, so minor.

results.quote: Hardest join: which two accountabilities met in the decisions that waited longest or were reopened?
results.finding: Both readers noted that the chapter defines exactly two accountabilities, so the join inside engineering (two jobs) does not fit the word. Rated (b) by both, so minor.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Make the Executive Team the First Team ¶4
results.quote: Which teams exist, what each owns and who is the director of each product group
results.finding: Reader B only, rated (a); the quote is from the page table as reader B reports it (the table text is not in structure.json). The scene had engineering directors in one drawing and a product lead per group in the other, and the reader could not tell what a product-group director is in a chart that 'kept two lines'. The spec's open questions already flag the director-per-group point, so the fault is not clearly the draft's.

results.quote: The same question gives a rule for the three other heads: a function reports where its decisions most often need to be joined with others.
results.finding: Reader B rated the order among design, data and security 'unclear'; reader A inferred it from the role table. The spec declares a reason for design coming first (its decisions meet product decisions most directly) that the draft does not state, while data and security each say why they follow. One reader only, so minor.

Every term on does_not_know is explained at or before first substantive use: joined decision and configuration are defined in bold, CTO, CPO and CPTO are expanded, the VP Engineering is defined in the role table, first team and structured escalation are defined with their sources; Founder Queue, Throne Room and Review Bottleneck are glossed where used. Neither flow reader reported an unexplained term.
The introduction opens on a specific scenario, bridges from the reader's experience, states a disputable claim and a route; none of the weak patterns is present.

The conclusion sorts its points by how settled they are, adds the reading of Corvane's three failures as unwritten joins, gives a checklist and a hand-off; it has no formulaic opener, no new subtopic and no body evidence, and it does more than rephrase the thesis.

The synthesis is present (three configurations as three places to put one join; what failed each time was an unwritten join), and the so-what is given as action: start from the last two quarters' joined decisions, put a person or written agreement on the hardest, state a role made for a person as a cost.

The closing paragraph returns to the two drawings, says they asked who leads a team and that the answer that worked was a list of who decides what, then hands the last row of that list to the next chapter.

The intro reader predicted the claim, the three configurations with their conditions and the section order exactly as the roadmap and the spec have them. The points left open (how the dispute resolves, what AI changes) are things an introduction may withhold.

The probe reader proposed a VP Engineering to run the organization under the founder CTO and a product executive to take product decisions off the CEO, and named the loss of speed and of a single point of joining, with the new joins to be written down; this matches the expected answer. The reader noted that the chapter never treats a CEO-led product arrangement directly and inferred it from the Throne Room and the 2023-2024 row.

Design, data and security have one section each, and each has a paragraph saying how little the sources offer ('My sources add little here', 'do not treat the data executive at all', 'mention security only in passing') and marking the rest as the author's judgment.

Both patterns name a user and an outcome measure: whoever designs the top (CEO, founders or board), with joined decisions made faster and fewer reopened or made by one side; and the two peer executives, with disagreements reaching the CEO from both at once and settled decisions staying settled.
